items.stem: In Kleinman's model of the health care system, where are most episodes of sickness first managed?
items.answer: The popular sector of family and community
items.markingKey: The popular sector of family and community. Self-treatment and family advice handle most sickness.

items.stem: Distinguish between a naturalistic explanation of sickness and a personalistic explanation of sickness.
items.answer: A personalistic explanation attributes sickness to the actions of an agent such as a witch, spirit or ancestor; a naturalistic explanation attributes it to impersonal forces such as germs, humoral imbalance or cold (George Foster, 1976).
items.markingKey: A personalistic explanation attributes sickness to the actions of an agent such as a witch, spirit or ancestor; a naturalistic explanation attributes it to impersonal forces such as germs, humoral imbalance or cold (George Foster, 1976). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why conflicting explanatory models can affect health outcomes.
items.answer: If doctors and patients disagree about cause and treatment, patients may not follow prescriptions or may seek other healers, and trust breaks down – as with Lia Lee's family and her doctors in Merced. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: If doctors and patients disagree about cause and treatment, patients may not follow prescriptions or may seek other healers, and trust breaks down – as with Lia Lee's family and her doctors in Merced. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Read the text below.

The doctor at the district clinic tells Grandfather Osei that his blood pressure is "very high" and gives him tablets. On the walk home he tells his grandson that the pressure comes from "thinking too much" since his land was taken by his nephew. He takes the tablets only on days when he has quarrelled. His grandson, a nursing student, explains that the tablets must be taken daily. "The tablets are for the body," the old man replies. "The thinking needs a family meeting." The following week, the elders call the nephew to a meeting.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a rural district in Ghana.

Describe how Grandfather Osei understands and responds to his high blood pressure, as presented in the text. You do not need to refer to any other ethnography in this answer.
items.answer: He receives tablets for "very high" blood pressure; he attributes it to "thinking too much" after his nephew took his land; he takes tablets only on days he has quarrelled; he says the tablets are for the body but the thinking needs a family meeting; the elders call the nephew to a meeting.
items.markingKey: He receives tablets for "very high" blood pressure; he attributes it to "thinking too much" after his nephew took his land; he takes tablets only on days he has quarrelled; he says the tablets are for the body but the thinking needs a family meeting; the elders call the nephew to a meeting. Award 1 mark per relevant descriptive point supported by the text (or 2 for a point developed with a quotation or specific detail), up to [4]. Description only is required; do not credit outside ethnography in this question.

items.stem: With reference to Emily Martin, The Woman in the Body: A Cultural Analysis of Reproduction (1987), explain how the key concept of power helps us to understand the experience and explanation of sickness.
items.answer: Middle-class women tended to accept the medical model of their bodies, while working-class women more often resisted it.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Middle-class women tended to accept the medical model of their bodies, while working-class women more often resisted it. Award up to [4]: 1 mark for accurate ethnographic context (Emily Martin, The Woman in the Body: A Cultural Analysis of Reproduction (1987), among women in Baltimore, USA, and in medical textbooks); further marks for specific ethnographic detail and an explicit, developed link to power. Credit another accurate ethnography if the question allows it.

items.stem: A student claims: "If a disease is diagnosed correctly, the patient's beliefs about it are irrelevant." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Beliefs shape how patients experience illness, whether they follow treatment and how they seek care, so they affect outcomes.
items.markingKey: Beliefs shape how patients experience illness, whether they follow treatment and how they seek care, so they affect outcomes. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Biomedicine is simply more correct than other medical systems."
items.answer: Biomedicine is highly effective for many diseases, but its practice is cultural and it does not address all dimensions of illness.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: biomedicine has proven efficacy for many diseases (antibiotics, vaccines); it rests on experimental evidence. Arguments against: it is also a cultural system with its own metaphors and biases (Martin, Lock); other systems address meaning and social relations; efficacy depends on access and trust. Supported judgement: Biomedicine is highly effective for many diseases, but its practice is cultural and it does not address all dimensions of illness.

items.stem: "Power is central to understanding the experience and explanation of sickness." Compare and contrast two anthropological studies, for example Martin's The Woman in the Body and Evans-Pritchard's Witchcraft, Oracles and Magic among the Azande, in the light of this claim.
items.answer: Martin's The Woman in the Body (among women in Baltimore, USA, and in medical textbooks): Middle-class women tended to accept the medical model of their bodies, while working-class women more often resisted it. Evans-Pritchard's Witchcraft, Oracles and Magic among the Azande (among the Azande of the southern Sudan (fieldwork 1926–1930)): The verdicts of princes' poison oracles were final, so control over divination supported political authority. Similarities and differences should be made explicit, e.g. how far power is imposed by wider structures or negotiated by the people themselves in each context, and how the methods and theoretical approach of each ethnographer shape the account.

Evans-Pritchard's Witchcraft, Oracles and Magic among the Azande (among the Azande of the southern Sudan (fieldwork 1926–1930)): The verdicts of princes' poison oracles were final, so control over divination supported political authority. items.stem: Explain why the distinction between disease and illness is useful for anthropologists.
items.answer: It separates the biological condition diagnosed by practitioners from the patient's experience and meaning of being unwell, showing why people with the same disease may suffer differently and why treatment that ignores illness may fail.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It separates the biological condition diagnosed by practitioners from the patient's experience and meaning of being unwell, showing why people with the same disease may suffer differently and why treatment that ignores illness may fail. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why biomedicine can be analysed as a cultural system.
items.answer: Biomedicine has its own categories, metaphors, rituals and hierarchies (e.g. Martin's industrial metaphors for the female body), and its practice varies between countries (Lock on menopause), so it is not a culture-free view from nowhere.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Biomedicine has its own categories, metaphors, rituals and hierarchies (e.g. Martin's industrial metaphors for the female body), and its practice varies between countries (Lock on menopause), so it is not a culture-free view from nowhere. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "Explanatory models are only held by patients from non-Western cultures." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Everyone, including biomedical doctors, holds explanatory models; Kleinman applied the concept to practitioners as well as to patients.
items.markingKey: Everyone, including biomedical doctors, holds explanatory models; Kleinman applied the concept to practitioners as well as to patients. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly describe the case of Lia Lee in Fadiman's The Spirit Catches You and You Fall Down and explain what it reveals about conflicting explanatory models.
items.answer: Doctors in Merced treated Lia's epilepsy with complex drug regimes; her Hmong parents, who saw the seizures as qaug dab peg, adjusted the medicines and Lia was placed in foster care for a time. The breakdown came from incompatible explanatory models and unequal power, not simply non-compliance; Kleinman's questions were later used to train doctors in cultural competence.
items.markingKey: Context (Doctors in Merced treated Lia's epilepsy with complex drug regimes; her Hmong parents, who saw the seizures as qaug dab peg, adjusted the medicines and Lia was placed in foster care for a time.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: the breakdown came from incompatible explanatory models and unequal power, not simply non-compliance; Kleinman's questions were later used to train doctors in cultural competence. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to conflicting explanatory models.

items.stem: Respond to the big question "Is culture something people have, or something people do?" by drawing on the experience and explanation of sickness, the concept of culture and E. E. Evans-Pritchard, Witchcraft, Oracles and Magic among the Azande (1937) or another ethnography.
items.answer: A strong answer takes a position on the big question, applies culture explicitly and uses ethnography: Witchcraft explains the particular misfortune: Azande know that termites ate the supports of a granary, but witchcraft explains why it collapsed when particular people were sitting beneath it. It weighs a contrasting perspective (another ethnography or theory) and reaches a reasoned conclusion.

items.stem: Define the term "embodiment".
items.answer: The idea that social experience, culture and inequality are lived and expressed through the body
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the idea that social experience, culture and inequality are lived and expressed through the body. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Kenji writes: "Culture-bound syndromes are not real illnesses." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: They involve genuine suffering and recognised symptoms; what is culturally specific is how distress is expressed, named and treated.
items.markingKey: They involve genuine suffering and recognised symptoms; what is culturally specific is how distress is expressed, named and treated. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between the individual and the dividual.
items.answer: The individual is a bounded, autonomous self, as in Western thought; the dividual is a person composed of relationships and shared substances, partible and exchanged, as described for Melanesia and South Asia.
items.markingKey: The individual is a bounded, autonomous self, as in Western thought; the dividual is a person composed of relationships and shared substances, partible and exchanged, as described for Melanesia and South Asia. items.stem:
Read the text below.

After the earthquake, Doña Teresa's granddaughter stopped eating and slept all day. The clinic doctor said she was "depressed" and suggested pills. Doña Teresa called the curandera instead, who swept the girl's body with an egg and herbs and called her name at the place where the wall had fallen. "Her spirit stayed there when she ran," Doña Teresa explained. Three days later the girl asked for tortillas. Her mother, who works in the city, now keeps the clinic leaflet and the curandera's herbs on the same shelf.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a town in highland Guatemala.

Describe how the granddaughter's condition was understood and treated, as presented in the text. Focus on what the people in the text do and say, not on your interpretation of it.
items.answer: After the earthquake the girl stopped eating and slept all day; the doctor diagnosed depression and suggested pills; the curandera swept her body with an egg and herbs and called her name where the wall fell; Doña Teresa believed her spirit had stayed there; the girl recovered appetite after three days; the mother keeps both leaflet and herbs.

Explain how the text illustrates the relationship between the body, personhood and a culturally specific illness, using one or more anthropological concepts. Distinguish between what the text shows and what you infer from it.
items.answer: The girl's condition is understood as susto: a fright separated her spirit from her body, so personhood is seen as composed of body and spirit that can become detached; healing restores the person by calling the spirit back at the place of loss. The doctor's "depression" is a biomedical model; the mother's shelf shows pluralism.

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that the concept of culture-bound syndromes should be abandoned? Answer with reference to one ethnography in depth.
items.answer: The original concept is flawed, but the insight that distress is culturally shaped should be retained in reformulated terms.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: it exoticises non-Western suffering; Western conditions are also culture-bound; it draws attention to cultural variation in distress; DSM-5's "cultural concepts of distress" offers a more balanced replacement. Suitable ethnographies include Scheper-Hughes's Death without Weeping, Lock's Encounters with Aging, Ong's Spirits of Resistance and Capitalist Discipline. A strong answer reaches a judgement such as: The original concept is flawed, but the insight that distress is culturally shaped should be retained in reformulated terms. items.stem: In north-east Brazil, Scheper-Hughes found that hunger was often reinterpreted as:
options: nervos, a nervous illness treated with tranquillisers
koro, a fear of genital retraction
susto, a soul loss
amok, a violent frenzy
items.answer: nervos, a nervous illness treated with tranquillisers
items.markingKey: A. The medicalisation of hunger hid its political causes.

items.stem: Explain why anthropologists say the body is shaped by society.
items.answer: Diet, labour, violence and medical intervention leave marks on bodies (Holmes's injured pickers, Scheper-Hughes's nervos), and cultural meanings shape how bodies are experienced and displayed.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Diet, labour, violence and medical intervention leave marks on bodies (Holmes's injured pickers, Scheper-Hughes's nervos), and cultural meanings shape how bodies are experienced and displayed. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Outline one way in which Scheper-Hughes on nervos in the Alto do Cruzeiro shows the body politic and embodiment.
items.answer: Exhausted, hungry sugar-cane workers and their families complained of nervos – trembling, weakness, headaches – and clinics prescribed tranquillisers and vitamins. Hunger produced by inequality was turned into an individual nervous illness, depoliticising suffering written on the body.
items.markingKey: Context (Exhausted, hungry sugar-cane workers and their families complained of nervos – trembling, weakness, headaches – and clinics prescribed tranquillisers and vitamins.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: hunger produced by inequality was turned into an individual nervous illness, depoliticising suffering written on the body. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the body politic and embodiment.

items.stem: With reference to Margaret Lock, Encounters with Aging: Mythologies of Menopause in Japan and North America (1993), explain how the key concept of materiality helps us to understand the body and culturally specific illness.
items.answer: Lock coined "local biologies" to show that bodily experience itself differs between populations through the interaction of biology, diet and culture.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Lock coined "local biologies" to show that bodily experience itself differs between populations through the interaction of biology, diet and culture. With reference to the text and to professional guidelines such as the AAA Principles of Professional Responsibility, discuss the ethical responsibilities of the anthropologist. Consider the ethics of publication as well as of the fieldwork itself.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A South Asian medical system, set out in texts such as the Charaka Samhita, that explains health as a balance of three doshas – vata, pitta and kapha"?
options: Ayurveda
efficacy
shaman
the three bodies
items.answer: Ayurveda
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of Ayurveda.

items.stem: Explain the difference between Ayurveda and biomedicine.
items.answer: Ayurveda explains health as the balance of doshas, treated through diet, herbs and lifestyle; biomedicine explains disease through pathogens and physiology. In India they coexist and Ayurveda is professionalised in state colleges.
items.markingKey: Ayurveda explains health as the balance of doshas, treated through diet, herbs and lifestyle; biomedicine explains disease through pathogens and physiology. In India they coexist and Ayurveda is professionalised in state colleges. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why healers derive authority from more than technical skill.
items.answer: Their authority depends on recognition by the community, initiation, lineage, spiritual calling or professional credentials, and on success stories that reinforce collective belief (Quesalid).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Their authority depends on recognition by the community, initiation, lineage, spiritual calling or professional credentials, and on success stories that reinforce collective belief (Quesalid). (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly describe Janzen's study of therapy management in Lower Zaire and explain what it reveals about healing systems and social relations.
items.answer: Kin groups combined hospital medicine with prophets and nganga healers, choosing according to whether an illness was "of God" or "of people". Healers were chosen by family groups according to how the illness was explained, showing healing as a social process.
items.markingKey: Context (Kin groups combined hospital medicine with prophets and nganga healers, choosing according to whether an illness was "of God" or "of people".) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: healers were chosen by family groups according to how the illness was explained, showing healing as a social process. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to healing systems and social relations.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

In the Ayurvedic clinic in Kochi, Dr Menon takes Mr Rao's pulse for several minutes before speaking. "Your pitta is high," she says, recommending he stop eating fried fish at night and take a herbal paste. Mr Rao, an engineer with diabetes, also takes metformin from his endocrinologist. He tells me: "The English doctor fixes the sugar number. Dr Menon fixes why I feel hot and angry all the time." On the clinic wall hang both a portrait of the god Dhanvantari and Dr Menon's degree certificate from the state Ayurveda college.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from an Ayurvedic clinic in Kerala, India.

With reference to the concept of culture, analyse why Mr Rao uses both Ayurveda and biomedicine. You may consider more than one possible interpretation of the evidence.
items.answer: He sees the systems as treating different aspects: biomedicine treats the disease measured as a number (blood sugar), while Ayurveda treats his illness experience (feeling hot and angry) through dosha balance and lifestyle. Dr Menon's authority combines religious symbolism (Dhanvantari) and professional credentials, showing the legitimacy of a professionalised healing system in medical pluralism.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: He sees the systems as treating different aspects: biomedicine treats the disease measured as a number (blood sugar), while Ayurveda treats his illness experience (feeling hot and angry) through dosha balance and lifestyle. Dr Menon's authority combines religious symbolism (Dhanvantari) and professional credentials, showing the legitimacy of a professionalised healing system in medical pluralism. items.stem: With reference to two anthropological studies, such as Kleinman's Patients and Healers in the Context of Culture and Lévi-Strauss's structuralism, compare and contrast the role of social relations in the work of healers.
items.answer: Kleinman's Patients and Healers in the Context of Culture (among patients, families, shamans (tâng-ki) and doctors in Taiwan (fieldwork 1969–1978)): Healing is a social process: families negotiate which practitioner to consult and how to interpret symptoms. Lévi-Strauss's structuralism (in comparative analyses of kinship and of Amerindian myths from South America): In alliance theory, the incest taboo forces groups to exchange women in marriage, creating bonds between groups; the taboo marks the passage from nature to culture. Similarities and differences should be made explicit, e.g. how far social relations is imposed by wider structures or negotiated by the people themselves in each context, and how the methods and theoretical approach of each ethnographer shape the account.

items.stem: A student claims: "Biomedicine involves no ritual or symbolism." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Biomedicine has rituals (ward rounds, white coats, prescriptions) and symbols that shape patients' experience and trust.

items.stem: Outline how culture shapes the work of healers, using evidence from Lévi-Strauss's structuralism.
items.answer: Lévi-Strauss argued that the human mind orders the world through binary oppositions such as raw/cooked and nature/culture, and that myths work through these oppositions.

items.answer: In Allan Young's usage, the social role and recognition of being unwell – how a society labels and responds to disease and illness

the three bodies

items.stem: Lévi-Strauss's "The Effectiveness of Symbols" analyses a song sung by a Guna (Cuna) shaman of Panama to:

bring rain

items.answer: help a woman through a difficult childbirth

items.stem: Distinguish between disease and illness.
items.answer: Disease is the biological malfunction diagnosed by practitioners; illness is the lived experience and cultural meaning of being unwell for the sufferer and their family.

items.stem: Explain why the concept of culture-bound syndromes has been criticised.
items.answer: It implied that only non-Western societies have culturally specific illnesses, whereas conditions like anorexia nervosa or premenstrual syndrome are also shaped by Western culture; it can also exoticise distress and obscure its social causes.

items.stem: "Biomedicine involves no ritual or symbolism." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Biomedicine has rituals (ward rounds, white coats, prescriptions) and symbols that shape patients' experience and trust.

items.stem: Explain the difference between the social body and the body politic.
items.answer: The social body is the body used as a symbol to think about society (Douglas); the body politic refers to how bodies are regulated, disciplined and controlled by power and the state.

items.stem: Explain the difference between shamanism and biomedicine.
items.answer: Shamanism treats sickness through communication with spirits and ritual restoring cosmic and social order; biomedicine treats disease through biological diagnosis and pharmaceutical or surgical intervention. Both rely on authority, ritual and belief.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

The doctor at the district clinic tells Grandfather Osei that his blood pressure is "very high" and gives him tablets. On the walk home he tells his grandson that the pressure comes from "thinking too much" since his land was taken by his nephew. He takes the tablets only on days when he has quarrelled. His grandson, a nursing student, explains that the tablets must be taken daily. "The tablets are for the body," the old man replies. "The thinking needs a family meeting." The following week, the elders call the nephew to a meeting.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a rural district in Ghana.

items.answer: The doctor's model locates hypertension in the body and prescribes daily medication (disease); Grandfather Osei's model links his illness to a social conflict over land (personalistic and social cause) and so adapts the treatment; he combines biomedicine with a family meeting to treat the social cause, illustrating Kleinman's disease/illness distinction and medical pluralism within the popular sector.

items.stem: Using Lévi-Strauss's account of Quesalid as an example, explain the social basis of healing.
items.answer: Quesalid learned shamans' techniques, including hiding a tuft of down in the mouth and producing it bloody as the extracted sickness, and patients recovered under his care. His success shows that healing depends on the shared beliefs of patient, healer and community, not only on technique.

items.stem: Using Scheper-Hughes on nervos in the Alto do Cruzeiro as an example, explain the body politic and embodiment.
items.answer: Exhausted, hungry sugar-cane workers and their families complained of nervos – trembling, weakness, headaches – and clinics prescribed tranquillisers and vitamins. Hunger produced by inequality was turned into an individual nervous illness, depoliticising suffering written on the body.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "The concept of culture-bound syndromes should be abandoned."
items.answer: The original concept is flawed, but the insight that distress is culturally shaped should be retained in reformulated terms.

items.stem: "Symbolic healing is as effective as biomedical treatment." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Their efficacy cannot be compared on one scale; symbolic healing addresses meaning and suffering, biomedicine biological disease.

items.stem: Compare and contrast how power is shown in Margaret Lock, Encounters with Aging: Mythologies of Menopause in Japan and North America (1993) and Emily Martin, The Woman in the Body: A Cultural Analysis of Reproduction (1987).
items.answer: Lock's Encounters with Aging (comparing middle-aged women in Japan with women in Canada and the United States): North American medicine framed menopause as a deficiency disease requiring hormone therapy, whereas Japanese doctors placed more emphasis on women's family duties, so medical models carried moral and gendered expectations. In Kleinman's distinction, a biological or psychological malfunction as defined and diagnosed by practitioners, especially in biomedicine
The dominant medical system in industrialised societies, based on biology and laboratory science, treated by anthropologists as one cultural system among others
The lived, subjective experience of being unwell, shaped by culture, including how symptoms are perceived, named and endured

Scheper-Hughes and Lock's (1987) framework of the individual body, the social body (body as symbol) and the body politic (bodies regulated by power)
The cultural understanding of what makes someone a person – when personhood begins and ends, and how it is composed of body, soul and relationships

items.stem: Briefly explain why conflicting explanatory models can affect health outcomes.
items.answer: If doctors and patients disagree about cause and treatment, patients may not follow prescriptions or may seek other healers, and trust breaks down – as with Lia Lee's family and her doctors in Merced.

items.stem: Distinguish between the dividual and the individual.
items.answer: The individual is a bounded, autonomous self, as in Western thought; the dividual is a person composed of relationships and shared substances, partible and exchanged, as described for Melanesia and South Asia.

items.stem: Explain why anthropologists study healing systems rather than just medicines.

items.stem: Distinguish between a personalistic explanation of sickness and a naturalistic explanation of sickness.
items.answer: A personalistic explanation attributes sickness to the actions of an agent such as a witch, spirit or ancestor; a naturalistic explanation attributes it to impersonal forces such as germs, humoral imbalance or cold (George Foster, 1976).

items.stem: Briefly explain why ideas about personhood affect medical decisions.

"Her spirit stayed there when she ran," Doña Teresa explained. Three days later the girl asked for tortillas. Her mother, who works in the city, now keeps the clinic leaflet and the curandera's herbs on the same shelf.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a town in highland Guatemala.

Compare and contrast how identity is experienced by the people in the text and by the people in one other ethnography you have studied (for example Margaret Mead, Coming of Age in Samoa (1928)). Consider how the methods or theory of the ethnography might explain the differences.
items.answer: Text: The girl's condition is understood as susto: a fright separated her spirit from her body, so personhood is seen as composed of body and spirit that can become detached; healing restores the person by calling the spirit back at the place of loss. The doctor's "depression" is a biomedical model; the mother's shelf shows pluralism. Ethnography – Margaret Mead, Coming of Age in Samoa (1928), among adolescent girls on Ta'ū in the Manu'a Islands of American Samoa (fieldwork 1925–1926): Mead described girls' identities as shaped by communal child-rearing and relaxed attitudes to sexuality, which she contrasted with the conflicts of American adolescence. Comparison: similarities and differences in how identity is produced, expressed or contested in the two settings, with explicit links between them.

items.stem: Respond to the big question "How are inequalities written onto human bodies?" by drawing on the work of healers, the concept of power and Arthur Kleinman, Patients and Healers in the Context of Culture (1980) or another ethnography.
items.answer: A strong answer takes a position on the big question, applies power explicitly and uses ethnography: When explanatory models clash, biomedical practitioners often discount patients' models, which affects trust, adherence and satisfaction. items.stem:
Read the text below.

The doctor at the district clinic tells Grandfather Osei that his blood pressure is "very high" and gives him tablets. On the walk home he tells his grandson that the pressure comes from "thinking too much" since his land was taken by his nephew. He takes the tablets only on days when he has quarrelled. His grandson, a nursing student, explains that the tablets must be taken daily. "The tablets are for the body," the old man replies. "The thinking needs a family meeting." The following week, the elders call the nephew to a meeting.
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a rural district in Ghana.

Discuss the ethical issues an anthropologist would need to consider when carrying out the fieldwork described in the text. Consider the ethics of publication as well as of the fieldwork itself.
items.answer: Health information is confidential; the land dispute is a sensitive family matter; the grandson's dual position as nursing student and family member must be considered; anonymise the family and clinic. General principles: informed and ongoing consent; do no harm; anonymity and confidentiality (pseudonyms, protecting data); weighing obligations to participants, funders and the public; reflexivity about the researcher's power and representation of people.

items.stem: "Is resistance always possible?" With reference to Martin's The Woman in the Body and the key concept of power, evaluate possible answers to this question.
items.answer: A strong answer takes a position on the big question, applies power explicitly and uses ethnography: Middle-class women tended to accept the medical model of their bodies, while working-class women more often resisted it. It weighs a contrasting perspective (another ethnography or theory) and reaches a reasoned conclusion.
